prose: Overall rate of choosing option B sits near chance across all trials, the expected balance for a symmetric choice set and a first integrity check on the raw data.
B is chosen least often where it is worst in expected value, the low end of the monotonic value gradient confirming choices track expected value.
B is chosen most often where it is best in expected value, the high end of the same gradient; together the extreme bins confirm value-sensitivity as designed.

Simulated participants with known parameters are recovered near-perfectly for EV sensitivity, establishing that the estimator can see individual differences in this parameter when they are genuinely present.
The risk-attitude parameter is likewise well recovered in simulation, so its later low empirical reliability cannot be attributed to the estimator.
Loss aversion is the least sharply recovered of the three even in simulation, though still above the pre-specified gate: the estimator detects it when present, but least well.

At the group level the model-agnostic EV index and the fitted EV coefficient agree strongly in the same sample; this convergent-validity bar is qualified by the cross-half addendum below, which shows most of the agreement reflects shared sample rather than independent estimation.

The model-agnostic risk index and the fitted risk coefficient agree only weakly (below the pre-specified convergent-validity bar), so the agnostic index is not a dependable proxy for the risk parameter.

The model-agnostic loss-avoidance index and the fitted loss coefficient are essentially unrelated (slightly negative), a clear failure of the convergent-validity bar, indicating the two operationalizations of loss aversion capture different things.

Across independent halves the agnostic EV index and the fitted EV coefficient barely agree, the honest cross-half counterpart to the strong same-sample figure, showing that apparent agreement largely does not survive independent estimation.
Within the same half the two EV measures agree moderately; the gap between this and the near-zero cross-half value localizes the earlier strong agreement to shared-sample information.
Across independent halves the adjusted loss-avoidance index and the fitted loss coefficient show effectively no agreement, reinforcing that the two loss operationalizations diverge.
Even within the same half the two loss measures do not agree, so their divergence is not merely a cross-half stability problem.
The central result: on the strict pool none of the five constructs reaches the conventional reliability bar at any budget the data provide.

The single measurement success on the strict pool: the adjusted loss-avoidance index reaches the lower reliability mark at a modest problem count, the only construct-and-pool combination to cross even that lower bar.
The reliability actually attained at that crossing sits just past the lower mark, illustrating how shallow even the best strict-pool measurement is.
Under the description regime (no feedback) the same index needs somewhat more problems to reach the lower mark than under experience, a robustness check on the experience-based curves.
A non-monotonic dip in one reliability curve is shown to be an artifact of which problems enter the sampled set, not a real reversal: reliability is monotone once the pool is held fixed.

Prior positive benchmark: a calibrated gamble-versus-sure task reports moderate test-retest reliability for loss aversion, placed on our common axis at its large per-participant design budget (direction-level comparison only).
The same study's risk-aversion test-retest is higher still, the strongest positive anchor in the cross-study comparison, sitting far to the right on the problem-count axis.

The strongest negative anchor for loss aversion: large-scale simulation finds the accept-reject parameter poorly recoverable however many trials are collected, the task-format-and-tradeoff channel of our necessary-but-not-sufficient reading.

The companion negative anchor establishing the problem-mix channel: the loss parameter fails to generalize across choice sets, the cross-study analogue of the curve shift we observe between our two pools.
Framing anchor on task format: risk preferences agree only weakly across elicitation methods within the same participants, consistent with elicitation format shaping the measure.
Framing anchor on temporal stability: behavioral risk measures show only moderate six-month retest, well below self-report, the reliability ceiling the field operates under.

Meta-analytic framing anchor: across many samples behavioral decision measures are substantially less temporally stable than self-report, situating our single-dataset findings in the wider literature.
The expanded pool's lottery reconstruction reproduces the official CPC18 implementation exactly, licensing the multi-outcome problems used to vary problem mix.
Every pinned official code and data artifact matches its recorded checksum: provenance integrity for the reconstruction.
On the expanded design EV-sensitivity recovery is near-perfect in simulation, arguing against a simple implementation failure on the richer pool as well.
Risk-attitude recovery on the expanded design is likewise high in simulation.
Loss-aversion recovery on the expanded design is high in simulation too, so empirical unreliability is not an estimator artifact on either pool.

Expressed as problems per half, the loss-avoidance index reaches the lower reliability mark on the expanded pool at the per-half budget corresponding to its total-problem crossing reported elsewhere; the richer mix pushes the budget outward.
The loss-avoidance index never reaches the conventional bar even on the expanded pool within the realized budgets: the pattern holds on the richer pool too.
The fitted EV coefficient does not reach the conventional bar anywhere on the expanded grid.
The fitted risk coefficient does not reach the conventional bar on the expanded grid.
The fitted loss coefficient does not reach the conventional bar on the expanded grid.

Pooled across the competition's problem forms, the model-agnostic EV index does not reach the conventional bar on the expanded grid; within a single form its between-person true-score variance is not distinguishable from zero, so its pooled reliability partly reflects differences between forms.
Even the best-measured construct, adjusted loss avoidance, does not reach the conventional bar on the expanded grid, completing the pattern across all five constructs and both pools.

By the largest expanded budget the EV coefficient, flat at strict-pool budgets, has climbed to partial measurability while remaining short of the conventional bar: the clearest single demonstration that problem mix, not merely count, moves reliability.
At a comparable strict-pool budget the same EV coefficient is essentially unmeasurable, the baseline against which the expanded-pool rise is read.
The independent choices13k dataset reproduces expected-value monotonicity at the aggregate problem level, a convergent check on choice patterns, not on individual differences.
choices13k reproduces the near-chance overall choice rate at the aggregate level, corroborating basic choice behavior across datasets.
The aggregate rate-versus-EV curve matches almost perfectly between datasets: strong convergent evidence at the population level only.

Exploratory only: at expected-value parity, aggregate choices in choices13k lean away from the loss-carrying option, a population-level loss-avoidance tendency, explicitly not an individual-difference reliability claim.
Exploratory only: the same population-level lean away from the loss option appears in aggregated CPC18 problems, the aggregate signal that must not be conflated with per-participant reliability.
